### **18.2 Lists**

> **CONCEPT: A list is a collection that stores its elements in an ordered sequence. Each element in a list can be accessed by its index, which is its position in the list**.

A list is an object that stores elements in an ordered sequence. A list works like an array of an unfixed size. As you add elements to a list, it dynamically grows in size to accommodate the new elements.

Each element in a list can be accessed by its index, which is its position in the list. The first element in a list is stored at position 0, so its index is 0\. The next element’s index is 1, and so forth. When you add an element to a list, you can append it to the end of the list, or you can insert it at a specific position. Elements at specific positions can also be removed from a list. Duplicate elements can be stored in a list.

#### **The `List` Interface**

The `List` interface specifies the operations that a list must support. It extends the `Collection` interface, so it inherits all of the methods specified by `Collection`. It also adds additional methods specifically for working with lists. In a nutshell, the `List` interface specifies methods for the following:

> • Adding elements at a specific index

> • Retrieving an element from a specific index

> • Changing the value of an element at a specific index

> • Removing an element that is at a specific index

> • Searching for an element in the list and getting its index number

> • Retrieving a small part of the list as a sublist.

[Figure 18-4](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos2915319) shows a UML diagram for the `List` interface. The methods that are specified by the `List` interface are described in [Table 18-2](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos2915587).

**Figure 18-4** The `List` interface

![Image](images/01335.jpg)

**Table 18-2** Methods specified by the `List` interface

![Image](images/01336.jpg)

![Image](images/01337.jpg)

![Image](images/01338.jpg)

![Image](images/00005.jpg)

* * *

**NOTE:** The `List` interface inherits all of the methods in the `Collection` interface, including the following:

`  boolean add(E o)`
`  boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c)`

When these inherited methods are called on a `List` object, the elements that are added to the list are appended to the end of the list.

* * *

#### **The `AbstractList` Class**

The `AbstractList` class extends the `AbstractCollection` class, and implements the `List` interface. It serves as an abstract superclass for other list classes. The `AbstractList` class provides default method definitions for all of the `List` methods except `get` and `size`. (The `size` method is specified by the `Collection` interface.) These two methods must be implemented in classes that extend `AbstractList`.

#### **The `ArrayList` Class**

You’ve already encountered the `ArrayList` class, which is a concrete list class in the JCF. `ArrayList` extends the `AbstractList` class. The `ArrayList` class has all of the methods specified by the `List` and `Collection` interfaces, as well as constructors and some additional methods. [Table 18-3](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos2919729) describes these additional methods.

An `ArrayList` object can dynamically grow in size to accommodate the number of objects that are stored in it. Internally, the `ArrayList` class stores objects in an array. When you create an `ArrayList` object using the no-arg constructor, the object’s internal array will have ten elements. So, you can store ten objects in the `ArrayList` without causing it to resize itself. When you store the eleventh object in the `ArrayList`, however, it creates a new, larger internal array, and copies the contents of the original array to it. The eleventh object is then added to the new array.

**Table 18-3** Additional methods in the `ArrayList` class

#### **Using an Interface Variable to Reference a Collection Object**

Take a closer look at the statement in line 12 of [Code Listing 18-1](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos2920566)

`  List<String> nameList = new ArrayList<String>();`

Notice that `nameList` is a `List` variable, not an `ArrayList` variable. Because the `ArrayList` class implements the `List` interface, we can use a `List` variable to reference an `ArrayList` object. This is a common practice. By always using interface variables to reference collection objects, our code will be easier to maintain if it becomes necessary to use a different concrete class to create the object.

For example, recall from [Figure 18-1](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos2902157) that the `ArrayList, LinkedList`, and `Vector` classes implement the `List` interface. Each of these classes can be used to create a list. Internally, however, there are differences in the way that these classes handle list operations. (We will study the differences shortly.) Suppose we write a program that at first uses an `ArrayList` to store a large number of `String` objects. We use the following statement to instantiate the `ArrayList`:

`  List<String> myList = new ArrayList<String>();`

Also, assume that in the program we pass the `ArrayList` object as an argument to numerous methods. Each of the methods uses a `List` variable as a parameter, such as the following:

`  public void displayList(List<String> somelist)`
`  {`
*`method code here…`*
`  }`

Once we put the program into use, we determine that the `ArrayList` is performing slowly because a large number of objects are constantly being inserted into it. After doing a little research, we determine that the `LinkedList` class performs faster under these circumstances, and we decide to use it instead of the `ArrayList` class. Because the `LinkedList` class also implements the `List` interface, and we have only used `List` variables to reference the `ArrayList`, making the change is simple. In the statement that instantiates the list object, we only have to change `ArrayList` to `LinkedList`, as shown here:

`  List<String> myList = new LinkedList<String>();`

Changes in other parts of the program are not necessary because we only used `List` variables to reference the list object.

#### **Using an Iterator to Get Elements from a List**

Previously we mentioned that an iterator is an object that can be used to retrieve the elements in a collection, one after the other. Recall that the `iterator` method in the `Collection` interface returns an `Iterator` object. `Iterator` is an interface in the JCF that specifies the basic operations that an iterator must perform. [Figure 18-5](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos2926403) shows a UML diagram for the `Iterator` interface, and [Table 18-4](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos2928028) describes the methods it specifies.

**Figure 18-5** The `Iterator` interface

![Image](images/01341.jpg)

Notice from [Table 18-2](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos2915587) that the `List` interface specifies the following two methods, each of which returns a reference to a `ListIterator` object:

`  ListIterator<E> listIterator()`
`  ListIterator<E> listIterator(int index)`

`ListIterator` is an interface in the JCF that extends the `Iterator` interface. A `ListIterator` object is a specialized type of iterator, made to work with a list. While an `Iterator` object can move in one direction only—forward, a `ListIterator` object can move through a list in either direction, forward or backward. [Figure 18-6](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos2928299) shows a UML diagram for the `ListIterator` interface and [Table 18-5](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos2929280) describes the methods it specifies.

**Table 18-4** Methods specified by the `Iterator` interface

![Image](images/01342.jpg)

**Figure 18-6** The `ListIterator` interface

![Image](images/01343.jpg)

When you need a list iterator to step through all of the elements in a list, you do not instantiate the list iterator yourself. Instead, you call one of the `List` object’s `listIterator` methods, which creates the list iterator for you. The list iterator that is returned from the `listIterator` method is ready to be used with the list. The program in [Code Listing 18-2](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos2929652) demonstrates how this is done with an `ArrayList`.

**Table 18-5** Methods specified by the `ListIterator` interface (in addition to those inherited from `Iterator`)

The statement in line 21 gets a reference to a list iterator from the `ArrayList` object, and assigns it to the `it` variable:

`  ListIterator it = nameList.listIterator();`

The list iterator that is returned from the `listIterator` method is ready to be used with the `ArrayList`. It is positioned at the first element in the `ArrayList`, as shown in [Figure 18-7](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos2932159). This is the element that will be returned from the list iterator’s `next` method the first time it is called.

The `while` loop that begins in line 24 iterates as long as the list iterator’s `hasNext` method returns `true`:

`  while (it.hasNext())`

The `hasNext` method returns `true` if a call to the `next` method will return a reference to an element. Inside the loop, in line 26, the list iterator’s `next` method is called, which returns a reference to an object. The reference is passed to `System.out.println`:

`  System.out.println(it.next());`

**Figure 18-7** The `ListIterator` positioned at the first element of the `ArrayList`

![Image](images/01346.jpg)

The first time the list iterator’s `next` method is called, the object containing `"Chris"` is returned and the list iterator’s position in the `ArrayList` is advanced to the next element. The list iterator is now positioned at the second element in the `ArrayList`, as shown in [Figure 18-8](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos2933104).

**Figure 18-8** The `ListIterator` positioned at the second element of the `ArrayList`

When the `next` method is called again, it will return a reference to the object that contains `"David"`, and the list iterator will be advanced to the third element. This process continues until the last element in the `ArrayList` has been returned by the `next` method. At that point, the list iterator will be positioned just beyond the last element in the `ArrayList`, as shown in [Figure 18-9](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos2935833). When the list iterator is in this position, a call to `hasNext` will return `false`, causing the loop to terminate.

**NOTE:** If you call the `next` method when the iterator is positioned beyond the last element in the list, the method will throw a `NoSuchElementException`.

You can also use a list iterator to move backward through a list. The `previous` method returns a reference to the previous node in the list. If the list iterator is at the beginning of the list when you call `previous`, then there are no previous elements and the method throws a `NoSuchElementException`. You can call the `hasPrevious` method to determine whether a previous element exists. The method returns `true` if a call to `previous` will return a reference to an element. The program in [Code Listing 18-3](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos2936193) demonstrates how to move forward and backward in an `ArrayList`.

#### **The Enhanced `for` Loop**

Recall from [Chapter 8](#dummy_split_015.html_filepos1408679) that Java provides an enhanced version of the `for` loop that simplifies the process of stepping through each element of an array. The enhanced `for` loop can also be used to step through each element of a collection. For example, the following code could be used to display each of the elements of the `ArrayList` in [Code Listing 18-3](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos2936193):

`  for (String element : nameList)`
`        System.out.println(element);`

When the Java compiler processes this code, it actually converts it to a traditional loop that uses an iterator.

#### **Using an Iterator to Modify a List**

List iterators provide three methods for modifying a list: `remove, add`, and `set`. Here is a summary of each method:

> • The `remove` method (which is specified in the `Iterator` interface) removes the last element that was returned by the `next` method.

> • The `add` method adds a new element to the list. The new element is added at the position immediately before the element that would be returned by a call to the `next` method.

> • The `set` method replaces an existing element with a new element. The element that is replaced is the last element that was returned from the iterator, using either the `next` or `previous` method.

The program in [Code Listing 18-4](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos2940017) demonstrates using the `add` method to insert an element into a list. In this program, the string `"Darlene"` is inserted immediately after `"Chris"` in our list of names.

#### **The `Vector` and `LinkedList` Classes**

So far we’ve only been using the `ArrayList` class to store objects in a list. In many situations that require a list, the `ArrayList` class is a good choice. The JCF also provides two other concrete list classes: `Vector` and `LinkedList`. Both of these classes implement the `List` interface. The differences between the `ArrayList, Vector`, and `LinkedList` classes are in the way they store and/or work with data. Your choice of which class to use will depend upon the nature of your application.

##### **The `Vector` Class**

The `Vector` class is essentially the same as the `ArrayList` class, except methods in the `Vector` class are *synchronized.* This means that the `Vector` class is safe to be used in a multithreaded application. A multithreaded application is one that concurrently runs multiple threads of execution. Each thread can carry out operations and access data in the program’s memory at the same time.

Problems can arise in a multithreaded application if two or more threads attempt to modify the same data, such as an element in an `ArrayList`, at the same time. There is a chance that the data will be corrupted. Because the `Vector` class’s methods are synchronized, they never simultaneously access an element in the `Vector`. This prevents the possibility of accidental data corruption.

The price that is paid for synchronization, however, is performance. Synchronization requires additional actions to be performed, and as a result, the `Vector` class is generally slower than the `ArrayList` class. If you are not developing a multithreaded application, then choose the `ArrayList` class instead of the `Vector` class. If you are developing a multithreaded application, however, and you want to be sure that none of the threads will concurrently access elements in a list, then use the `Vector` class.

The `Vector` class implements the `List` interface, and all of the methods that are found in the `ArrayList` class are also found in the `Vector` class.

![Image](images/00005.jpg)

* * *

**NOTE:** The `Vector` class has been part of Java for a long time, even before the JCF. Older pre-JCF versions of the `Vector` class used methods that performed the same operations as those specified by the `List` interface, but had different names. Today, the `Vector` class has the methods specified by the `List` interface and the older methods. The older methods were retained in the class for compatibility reasons.

* * *

##### **The `LinkedList` Class**

Unlike the `ArrayList` and `Vector` classes, the `LinkedList` class does not store its data in an array. Instead it uses a linked list. A *linked list* is a data structure made of a series of connected nodes. Each node in a linked list contains a data item (an element in the list) and a reference to the next node in the list. [Figure 18-10](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos2947480) shows how a linked list is organized. The list in the figure has three nodes. Notice that the last node in the list contains a null reference. This signifies the end of the list.

**Figure 18-10** Organization of a linked list

![Image](images/01357.jpg)

A linked list has some advantages over an array. First, if an array is full and you want to add an additional element to the end of it, you must create a new, larger array, and copy the elements from the old array to it. Then you can add data to the end of the new array. This is not necessary with a linked list, because a linked list does not have a fixed size. When a new node is added to the end of a linked list, the node is simply created in memory and then the last node in the list is made to reference it. This adds the new node to the end of the list.

Also, inserting a node into the middle of a linked list is much more efficient than inserting an element into the middle of an array. When an element is inserted into the middle of an array, all of the elements that come after the insertion point must be shifted toward the end of the array to make room for the new element. For example, suppose we have an array of 500 objects, and we want to insert a new object at index 50. All of the existing elements, from index 50 through 499 must be copied to the next element so the new object can be inserted at index 50\. To further slow things down, if the array is full when the insertion is made, first a new array must be created, and then each of the old elements copied to it. None of this is necessary with a linked list. When a new node is inserted into the middle of a linked list, only a few references are changed. [Figure 18-11](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos2949762) illustrates how a new node can be inserted between the second and third nodes of a linked list.

As you might imagine, removing an element from the middle of an array is also inefficient. All of the elements that appear after the removed element must be shifted toward the front of the array to take up the space. Removing a node from the middle of a linked list is a simple matter of adjusting a few references.

**Figure 18-11** A new node inserted into a linked list

![Image](images/01358.jpg)

![Image](images/00005.jpg)

* * *

**NOTE:** The linked list that is maintained internally by the `LinkedList` class is slightly more complex than the one shown in Figures 18-10 and 18-11\. The `LinkedList` class keeps a doubly-linked list, where each node in the list references both the previous node and the next node.

* * *

Because of its efficiency at inserting and removing nodes, the `LinkedList` class is a good choice when your application will be storing a large amount of data in a list, and a lot of insertions and/or deletions are likely to take place.

If you look back at [Figure 18-1](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos2902157), you will see that the `LinkedList` class extends the `AbstractSequentialList` class. Unlike an array, a linked list provides only sequential access to its elements. For example, you cannot randomly jump from one index to another in a linked list the way you can in an array. Some of the methods in the `AbstractList` class are implemented in a way that is suited best for a random-access structure like an array. So, the `AbstractSequentialList` class provides alternate implementations of the `List` methods, suited for sequential-access structures like a linked list.

The `LinkedList` class has all of the methods that are specified by the `List` and `Collection` interfaces, as well as constructors and some additional methods. [Table 18-6](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos2953602) describes the `LinkedList` constructors, and some of the additional methods it provides.

The *LinkedListDemo1.java* program, available for download from [www.pearsonhighered.com/gaddis](http://www.pearsonhighered.com/gaddis), shows a simple demonstration of the `LinkedList` class. This is a modification of the *ListIteratorDemo3.java* program in [Code Listing 18-4](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos2940017). The only difference is that this program uses a `LinkedList` instead of an `ArrayList`. The following code, which is excerpted from the program, shows the `LinkedList` being created and names added to it.

`  // Create a LinkedList to hold String objects.`
`  List<String> nameList = new LinkedList<String>();`

`  // Add some names to the list.`

`  nameList.add("David");`
`  nameList.add("Katherine");`
`  nameList.add("Kenny");`

#### **Summary of the Differences between the List Classes**

> • The `ArrayList` class internally uses an array to store its elements. It is a good choice when fast random access is important, only a minimum number of insertions and deletions will occur, and thread safety is not a concern.

> • The `Vector` class also uses an array internally to store its elements. The `Vector` class provides synchronized methods, however, so it is the choice to make in an application where multiple threads will have access to the list.

> • The `LinkedList` class internally stores its elements in a linked list. This is a good choice when the list will contain a large amount of data and numerous insertions and deletions will take place.

### **18.3 Sets**

> **CONCEPT: A set is a collection that lets you quickly find a value in a large amount of data. A set stores elements in an unordered sequence, and does not allow duplicates**.

Sometimes when data is stored in a list, you know the exact location of specific items. For example, suppose we have a list that holds the total sales for each month of the year. The list has twelve elements, with the indices 0 through 11\. We know that January’s sales amount is stored at index 0, February’s sales amount is stored at index 1, and so forth. If we want to retrieve the sales amount for December, we know that we have to retrieve the element at index 11\. In the list, the sales for month *n* is stored at index *n* − 1.

Sometimes we need to retrieve a particular element from a collection, but we do not know the location of that element. For example, suppose we have a collection of `Customer` objects, and we need to search for a particular object by the customer’s name. `Customer` objects are added to and removed from the collection on a daily basis, and we have no way of knowing where a particular object is stored. If the objects are stored in a list, finding a particular customer means sequentially searching the list until we find the element we are looking for. This could be a time-consuming process if there are a large number of objects in the list.

Perhaps a set is the best type of collection to use in this situation—if fast retrieval is important. Sets are useful when you have a large collection of data, and you must retrieve an element from the collection by searching for its value. The elements in a set are stored in a data structure that is optimized for this type of retrieval.

It is helpful to compare sets to lists. A list will allow you to append an element at the end, add an element at the beginning, or insert an element at a specific position within the list. In contrast, a set element is not associated with a position within the set. Sets are also different from lists in another way: they do not allow duplicate elements. Each element in a set must be unique.

#### **The `Set` Interface and the `AbstractSet` Class**

The `Set` interface extends the `Collection` interface, so it inherits all of the methods specified by `Collection`. (See [Table 18-1](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos2908257) for a description of the methods specified by the `Collection` interface.) The `Set` interface does not add any additional methods of its own, but it does place restrictions on many of the methods inherited from `Collection`. These restrictions enforce the requirement that a set cannot contain duplicate elements.

The `AbstractSet` class extends the `AbstractCollection` class, and implements the `Set` interface. This class can be used as an abstract superclass for other set classes, and all of the concrete set classes in the JCF extend this class.

#### **The `HashSet` Class**

The first concrete set class that we will study is the `HashSet` class, which implements the `Set` interface. The `HashSet` class uses hash codes to store its elements in a way that makes searching faster. To understand how a `HashSet` works, first you must understand the concept of a hash code.

A *hash code* is an integer value that is characteristic of an object. You use a *hashing algorithm* to calculate a hash code for an object. There are many different hashing algorithms, ranging from the simple to the complex. Although we will not conduct an in-depth study of hashing algorithms, later in this section we will look at some simple techniques for calculating hash codes.

Hashing algorithms typically use the data that is stored in an object to calculate the object’s hash code. For example, if we were to calculate the hash code for a string, we would somehow use the characters making up the string in the calculation. Perhaps we would use each character’s Unicode value in a mathematical formula that would give us an integer value. Ideally, our hashing algorithm would produce different hash codes for different strings. For example, the hash code for `"Fred"` would be different from the hash code for `"Wilma"`.

In addition to producing different hash codes for different objects, an ideal hashing algorithm should produce the same hash code for objects that are equal in value. For example, suppose we have the following two `String` objects, `str1` and `str2`:

`  String str1 = new String("Fred");`
`  String str2 = new String("Fred");`

Although `str1` and `str2` are different objects, they contain equal data and a hashing algorithm should produce the same hash code for both.

In Java, every object has a `hashCode` method that is inherited from the `Object` class. This method returns a hash code for the object. The `hashCode` method that is inherited from the `Object` class, however, is rarely adequate because it returns a value that is based on the object’s memory address. The value that is returned from the `Object` class’s `hashCode` method is unique for every object, even objects that contain the same data. For this reason, the `Object` class’s `hashCode` method must usually be overridden so that it returns the same hash code for equivalent objects.

Hash codes are at the heart of how the `HashSet` class works. When an object is added to a `HashSet`, the `HashSet` calls the object’s `hashCode` method to get its hash code. Then it checks to see if an object with the same hash code has already been stored in the set. (Remember, a set does not allow duplicates.) If it finds that an object with the same hash code is already in the set, it performs one more test: it calls the object’s `equals` method to see if it reports that the two objects are equal. If they are, the `HashSet` does not store the object in the set.

You might be wondering why a `HashSet` does not simply refuse to store an object as soon as it finds another object with the same hash code already in the set. Earlier we said that an ideal hashing algorithm would produce different hash codes for different values. That is true, but hashing algorithms are not usually ideal. Occasionally, a hashing algorithm will produce the same hash code for two objects that are not equal. This is called a *collision.* Because collisions can occur, the `HashSet` performs two tests, one using the `hashCode` method and the other using the `equals` method, to determine whether an object’s value is already in the set.

Because collisions sometimes occur with hashing algorithms, it is possible that when a new object is added to a `HashSet` it will have the same hash code as an object already in the set, but it will not be equal to that object (the two objects will contain different data). In this case, the `HashSet` must allow the new object to be added to the set.

One popular way of thinking about hash codes is that they identify “buckets” in the `HashSet`. Each individual hash code has its own bucket, and all objects in the set that have that hash code are stored in that hash code’s bucket. So, some buckets will have only one object stored in them, while other buckets will contain multiple objects. In pseudocode, the following is the procedure followed by the `HashSet` class to add a new object:

*Call the new object’s `hashCode` method to get the object’s hash code.*

*If that hash code’s bucket is empty, Then*

*Store the object in the bucket for that hash code.*

*Else*

*Use the object’s `equals` method to compare it to each object in the bucket.*

*If it is not equal to any other object in the bucket, Then*

*Store the object in the bucket.*

*Else*

*Do not store the new object.*

*End If*

*End If*

![Image](images/00006.jpg)

* * *

**TIP:** Because the `hashCode` and `equals` methods are used together like this, any time you override the `Object` class’s `equals` method you should also override the `hashCode` method.

* * *

The `HashSet` class has four constructors, which are summarized in [Table 18-7](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos2971767). Note that when a `HashSet` is constructed, it has an initial capacity and a load factor. The *initial capacity* is the number of “buckets” that the `HashSet` initially has. The *load factor* is the percentage of the buckets that have to be occupied before the capacity is increased. For example, with a load factor of 0.75, the capacity will be increased when 75 percent of the buckets have a value stored in them.

**Table 18-7** `HashSet` constructors

#### **Implementing Your Own `hashCode` Method**

When you design a class, you will need to override the `hashCode` and `equals` methods if you want to store objects of the class in a `HashSet`. Here are three guidelines that you should follow when writing your own `hashCode` and `equals` methods:

> 1\. If you call an object’s `hashCode` method more than once during the execution of an application, the method should consistently return the same value. The only exception is when something in the object has changed, which would affect the way the `equals` method makes comparisons.

> 2\. If the `equals` method reports that two objects are equal, then both objects’ `hashCode` methods should return the same value.

> 3\. If the `equals` method reports that two objects are *not* equal, it is permissible for both objects to have the same hash code. You should be aware, however, that having too many unequal objects with the same hash code will degrade the performance of an algorithm that uses the hash codes for searching.

The `String` class uses the following formula to calculate a hash code for a string:

*hashCode = S*[0] * 31^((*n* – 1))*+ S*[1] * 31^((*n* – 2)) + … + *S[n – 1]*

In the formula, *n* is the number of characters in the string, *S*[0] is the Unicode value of the character at position 0, *S*[1] is the Unicode value of the character at position 1, and *S[n – 1]* is the Unicode value of the character at position *n* − 1.

The algorithm used by the `String` class is moderately complex. Other classes use a simpler approach. For example, the `Character` class simply uses the character’s Unicode value as its hash code. The `Integer` class uses the actual integer value of the object as its hash code.

This should be adequate because each car has its own unique VIN. We have also overridden the `equals` method to return `true` if both objects have the same VIN.

#### **The `LinkedHashSet` Class**

You might have noticed that in the program output of Code Listings 18-6, 18-7, and 18-9, the order in which the `HashSet` elements are displayed does not match the order in which they were added to the set. Sets have no concept of internal position of their elements, and they do not keep track of the order of insertion. When you iterate through a `HashSet`, you should not expect the iterator to return elements in the order of their insertion.

If you need to access set elements in the order that they were inserted, you can use the `LinkedHashSet` class instead of `HashSet`. The `LinkedHashSet` class, which extends `HashSet`, keeps an internal linked list that references the elements of the set in the order that they were inserted. This gives you the ability of iterating through the set in that order.

The `LinkedHashSet` class’s constructors and methods are identical to those of the `HashSet` method. The program in [Code Listing 18-10](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos2983725) creates two sets: a `HashSet` and a `LinkedHashSet`. The same `String` objects are stored in each set.

#### **The `SortedSet` Interface and the `TreeSet` Class**

Looking back at the JCF hierarchy in [Figure 18-1](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos2902157), you will see that `SortedSet` is a subinter-face of the `Set` interface. A `SortedSet` is a set in which the elements are sorted in ascending order. [Table 18-8](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos2985218) summarizes the methods specified by the `SortedSet` interface.

**Table 18-8** `SortedSet` methods

![Image](images/01373.jpg)

The `TreeSet` class is a concrete class in the JCF that implements the `SortedSet` interface. The `TreeSet` class guarantees that when an iterator traverses the set, it will retrieve the elements in ascending order.

##### **Adding `Comparable` Objects to a `TreeSet`**

In order for a `TreeSet` to sort the objects that are stored in it, those objects must have a *natural order.* This means that the `TreeSet` must be able to compare the objects and determine whether one object is greater than, less than, or equal to the other. One way to accomplish this is to store only objects that implement the `Comparable` interface in the `TreeSet`. We discussed the `Comparable` interface in [Chapter 17](#dummy_split_024.html_filepos2759847), when we were studying generics. Recall that the `Comparable` interfaces specifies a method named `compareTo`, which is used to compare the calling object with another object that is passed as an argument to the method. This is how the `compareTo` method works:

> • If the calling object is less than the object passed as an argument, the method returns a negative number.

> • If the calling object is equal to the object passed as an argument, the method returns 0.

> • If the calling object is greater than the object passed as an argument, the method returns a positive number.

If you store only objects that implement the `Comparable` interface to a `TreeSet`, then the `TreeSet` can compare those objects with the `compareTo` method. In fact, when you create a `TreeSet` with its no-arg constructor, the `TreeSet` will assume that the objects you are adding to it implement `Comparable`. The program in [Code Listing 18-11](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos2988969) demonstrates this by creating a `TreeSet` and adding `String` objects to it. Recall that the `String` class implements the `Comparable` interface.

##### **Using a `Comparator` to Compare Objects**

If the objects that you wish to store in a `TreeSet` do not implement the `Comparable` inter-face, you can still store them in the `TreeSet` by creating a `Comparator`. A `Comparator` is an object that can compare two other objects and determine whether one is greater than, less than, or equal to the other. A `Comparator` implements the `Comparator` interface, which is in the `java.util` package. The `Comparator` interface is defined as follows:

### **18.4 Maps**

> **CONCEPT: Each element in a map has two parts: a key and a value. Each key is associated with a specific value, and can be used to locate that value**.

Each element in a *map* has two parts: a key and a value. Each key is associated with a specific value, and can be used to locate that value. For example, suppose we wish to store employee names in a map, and we want to search for specific employees by their ID numbers. Each time we store an employee’s name in the map as a value, we also store that employee’s ID number as a key. The map creates an association between the value and the key, and allows us to retrieve the name by searching for the ID number. The elements in a map are referred to as *mappings.*

Because keys are used to locate specific values, maps do not allow duplicate keys. Each key is mapped to one value. Maps do allow duplicate values, however.

#### **The `Map` Interface and the `AbstractMap` Class**

The `Map` interface specifies the fundamental operations that any map must support. There are methods for adding mappings, removing mappings, searching for values and for keys, and performing other operations on the map. [Figure 18-12](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos2999055) shows a UML diagram for the `Map` interface, and [Table 18-11](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos2999315) describes each method specified in the `Map` interface.

The `AbstractMap` class serves as a superclass for concrete classes that implement the `Map` interface. It only adds one additional method, `toString`, which returns a string representation of the map’s contents.

**Figure 18-12** The `Map` interface

![Image](images/01380.jpg)

**Table 18-11** Methods specified by the `Map` interface

![Image](images/01382.jpg)

#### **The `HashMap` Class**

The `HashMap` class is a concrete class that extends `AbstractMap` and implements the `Map` interface. Like a `HashSet`, a `HashMap` uses hash codes to store and retrieve data. Specifically, the `HashMap` class stores keys by their hash codes. [Table 18-12](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos3001912) summarizes the `HashMap` constructors. Some of these constructors will look familiar because they are similar to the `HashSet` constructors. Because the `HashMap` class uses hash codes to store keys, it provides constructors that allow you to specify initial capacity and load factor. (See the previous section on the `HashSet` class for a discussion of initial capacity and load factor.)

The statement in lines 13 and 14 creates the `HashMap`:

`  Map<String, Car> carMap =`
`        new HashMap<String, Car>();`

Both the `Map` interface and the `HashMap` class specify two generic type parameters: one for the key data type, and one for the value data type. That explains why we have specified two data types, `String` and `Car`, in the generic type notation. `String` is the data type of the keys, and `Car` is the data type of the values. This is illustrated in [Figure 18-13](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos3003891).

**Figure 18-13** Data types for keys and values specified

![Image](images/01386.jpg)

The statements in lines 17 through 20 create four `Car` objects: one for a VW, one for a Mustang, one for a Porsche, and one for a BMW. Then, the statements in lines 25 through 28 use the `put` method to create several mappings in the `HashMap`. For example, look at the statement in line 25:

`  carMap.put(vw.getVin(), vw);`

The `put` method puts a mapping into the `HashMap`. The first argument is the key, and the second argument is the value to associate with the key. In this program we are creating mappings between VINs and `Car` objects. In each mapping, the key is a VIN and the value is the `Car` object that goes with that VIN. In this statement we are creating a mapping that associates the VW’s VIN with the VW’s `Car` object. The statements in lines 26 through 28 create similar mappings for the other `Car` objects.

Line 33 shows how we can search for a specific `Car` object:

`  Car foundCar = carMap.get(mustang.getVin());`

This statement creates a `Car` reference variable, `foundCar`, and assigns to it the value returned from the `carMap.get` method. The `get` method accepts a key as its argument and it returns the value that the key is mapped to. In this statement we are passing the Mustang’s VIN as the argument. We are basically saying to the `HashMap` “Give me the `Car` object that is associated with this VIN.” If the key is found in the `HashMap`, the method returns a reference to the value that is associated with that key. Because the Mustang’s VIN is indeed found as a key in the `HashMap`, this statement returns a reference to the `mustang` object and assigns to `foundCar`.

In line 44 we aren’t so lucky. Here we pass to the get method a VIN that does not exist in the `HashMap`:

`  foundCar = carMap.get("911C87");`

As a result, the method will return `null`.

Maps do not provide iterators, so if you wish to iterate over the contents of a map, you will have to convert its mappings to some other type of collection. For example, you can use the `keySet` method to get a `Set` that contains all of the keys in a map, and you can use the `values` method to get a `Collection` that contains all of the map’s values. Then you can iterate over the resulting `Set` or `Collection`. [Code Listing 18-15](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos3008423) shows an example.

#### **The `LinkedHashMap` Class**

`HashMap`s are unordered, and, like sets, have no concept of position for their elements. For example, notice that the order in which the mappings are displayed in the output of [Code Listing 18-16](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos3011342) does not match the order in which they were put into the `HashMap`.

The `LinkedHashMap` class, which extends `HashMap`, allows you to access its mappings in one of two orders:

> • Insertion order, which is the order in which the mappings were inserted into the map

> • Access order, which is the order in which the mappings were last accessed

A `LinkedHashMap` keeps an internal linked list that references mappings. If you are using the map in insertion order mode, the linked list references the mappings in the order that they were inserted. If you are using the map in access order mode, the linked list references the mappings in the order that they were accessed with either `put` or `get`.

In access order mode, the mappings that have been accessed the most are placed at the end of the linked list, and the mappings that have been accessed the least are placed at the beginning. This mode is useful in applications that need to know which data items are being accessed the most or the least.

You indicate which sorting order you prefer with the appropriate `LinkedHashMap` constructor. [Table 18-13](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos3014908) summarizes them.

#### **In the Spotlight: Using Lists and Maps in Your Programs ![Image](images/00008.jpg)**

Since its earliest days, Java has allowed arrays to be initialized at the time they are declared if the contents to be stored in the array are known:

`  String[] colorNames = {"PINK", "YELLOW", "BLUE", "RED"};`
`  Color[] colors = {Color.PINK, Color.YELLOW, Color.BLUE, Color.RED};`

This is a great convenience to programmers. Recent versions of Java provide facilities that make it easy to initialize lists in a similar manner. Beginning with version 5, the `java.util.Arrays` class has a static generic method `asList` that can be used to turn an array into a list. The method can be called in two different ways: by passing it a single array parameter or by passing it comma-separated list of items. In the following code, both statements initialize a list to the same sequence of strings:

`  String [] numerals = {"one", "two", "three"};`
`  // Pass a single array as parameter`
`  List<String> list2 = Arrays.asList(numerals);`
`  // Pass any number of comma separated values as parameters`
`  List<String> list1 = Arrays.asList("one", "two", "three");`

If you know the set of keys and values that will be stored in a map, you can use a pair of parallel arrays and a loop to initialize the map. For example, suppose that you want to build a map that pairs names of colors given by an array `colorNames`, with color objects given by a second array `colors`. You can initialize the map as follows:

`  String[] colorNames = {"PINK", "YELLOW", "BLUE", "RED"};`
`  Color[] colors = {Color.PINK, Color.YELLOW, Color.BLUE, Color.RED};`
`  Map<String, Color> colorMap = new HashMap<String, Color>();`
`  for (int k = 0; k < colorNames.length; k++)`
`  colorMap.put(colorNames[k], colors[k]);`

### **18.6 Common Errors to Avoid**

> • **Not calling an iterator’s `hasNext` method before calling `next`**. To prevent an exception from being thrown, you should always call an iterator’s `hasNext` method before calling it’s `next` method. This ensures that the `next` method will actually return a reference.

> • **Not calling an iterator’s `next` method before calling `remove`**. An iterator’s `remove` method removes the last element that was returned by the `next` method. The `next` method must be called before the `remove` method can be called.

> • **Not calling a `ListIterator’s hasPrevious` method before calling `previous`**. To prevent an exception from being thrown, you should always call a `ListIterator`’s `hasPrevious` method before calling its `previous` method.

> • **Not calling a `ListIterator’s hasNext` or `hasPrevious` method immediately before calling `set`**. To prevent an exception from being thrown, you should always call a `ListIterator`’s `hasNext` or `hasPrevious` method before calling its `set` method.

> • **Modifying a collection via one of its methods after an iterator has been created for the collection**. After an iterator has been created for a collection, you cannot modify the collection using one of the collection’s methods, and then continue to use the iterator. Doing so will cause an exception to be thrown. If you wish to modify a collection while it is being iterated over, you should use the iterator to perform the modifications. For example, the `Iterator` interface specifies a `remove` method, and the `ListIterator` interfaces specifies `add` and `set` methods.

> • **Designing a class so objects of the class can be stored in a `HashSet`, but not overriding both the `equals` and `hashCode` methods**. When an object is stored in a `HashSet`, both the `hashCode` and the `equals` methods are used to find a location for the object in the `HashSet`. If you are designing a class so objects of the class can be stored in a `HashSet`, you should override both the `hashCode` and the `equals` methods.

> • **Storing objects that cannot be compared in a `TreeSet`**. In a `TreeSet`, objects are compared using the `compareTo` method. An error will occur if you attempt to store in a `TreeSet` an object of a class that does not implement the `compareTo` method.

> • **Attempting to store duplicate keys in a map**. The keys in a map must be unique.

Write an application that reads a line of input from the keyboard, and then displays each unique word that was entered, sorted in ascending order. You can do this by tokenizing the line of input and adding each token to an appropriate `Set` object.

**2\. Instructor Set**

(See Section 9.7—Aggregation) Modify the `Instructor` class by overriding the `hashCode` and `equals` methods. Then write a class that stores several `Instructor` objects in a `HashSet`. The class should be able to display all the instructors in the set, and allow the user to search for an instructor. Demonstrate the class in an application.

![Image](images/00010.jpg)

**3\. `EmployeeMap` Class**

Create an `Employee` class that stores an employee’s ID number and name. Then create an `EmployeeMap` class that allows you to add `Employee` objects and look them up by their ID numbers. The `EmployeeMap` class should use a `Map` object to map ID numbers to `Employee` objects. Create an application to demonstrate the classes.

**4\. Stock Map**

[Chapter 9](#dummy_split_016.html_filepos1621783) presented a `Stock` class that holds information about a stock. (See Section 9.4— The `toString` Method) Write a class that keeps `Stock` objects in a `Map`. The class should be able to retrieve a particular `Stock` object from the `Map` by searching on its stock symbol. Demonstrate the class in an application.

**5\. Prime Number List**

A prime number is a number that is only evenly divisible by itself and 1\. For example, the number 5 is prime because it can only be evenly divided by 1 and 5\. The number 6, however, is not prime because it can be divided evenly by 1, 2, 3, and 6\. Write an application that calculates and stores the first 100 prime numbers (starting at 1) in a list. Use an iterator to display the numbers.

**6\. Dealing Cards**

Write a class named `Card`, which can be used to represent a card from a deck of cards. The class should be able to store a card’s suit and face value. A card’s suit can be one of the following: Hearts, Diamonds, Spades, or Clubs. A card’s face value can be Ace, Jack, Queen, King, or a value in the range of two through ten.

Next write a `Deck` class. This class constructor should create a list of 52 `Card` objects, each representing a valid card in a deck of cards. The class should have a `shuffle` method that randomly shuffles the `Card` objects in the list. It should also have a `deal` method that “deals” a card from the deck. It does this by removing the `Card` object at the beginning of the list and returning a reference to that object.

Next, write `CardPlayer` class. This class should keep a list of `Card` objects that have been dealt to it. This represents a hand of cards. A method named `getCard` should accept a reference to a `Card` object, which is added to the list. A method named `showCards` displays the `Card` objects in the list.

Demonstrate these classes in an application that creates a `Deck` object, shuffles the cards it contains, and deals five cards from the `Deck` to a `CardPlayer` object. The `CardPlayer` should then display its cards.

**7\. `Action` and `AbstractAction`**

Java defines a subinterface of the `ActionListener` interface called `Action`. Among the methods that `Action` adds to `ActionListener` are

`  Object getValue(String key);`
`  void putValue(String key, Object value);`

These two methods assume the existence of a maplike structure that uses strings to access objects. Java provides an abstract class called `AbstractAction` that implements the methods in `Action`, leaving only the

`  void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e)`

method to be implemented by the programmer. Research the `AbstractAction` class online and then write a subclass of `AbstractAction` called `ColorAction` that maps names of colors to `Color` objects. Add an object of `ColorAction` as an `ActionListener` to the `JTextfield` to handle such `Action` events. ### **19.1 Introduction to Lists**

> **CONCEPT: A list is a container that holds objects as a group of elements**.

Without a doubt you are familiar with lists because they are so common. Before you go to the grocery store, you probably make a list of items to purchase. During a busy morning of running errands, you might make yourself a list of things to do. When you plan to throw a party, it’s usually a good idea to prepare a list of guests to invite. A list is simply a group of items that are stored together for some purpose.

Lists are also common in computer science. To the programmer, a list is a container that holds a group of elements. The elements in a list are stored in a sequence where one element is considered to come after the other. Typically, the elements in a list have an associated index, which corresponds with each element’s position in the list. The first element has the index 0, the second element has the index 1, and so forth. Each element except the last element has a *successor*, and each element except the first element has a *predecessor.* Lists also have a size, which is the number of elements that are stored in the list. In addition, lists have various methods that allow you to store, retrieve, and remove elements.

In [Chapter 18](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos2894334) you encountered the `List` types in the Java Collections Framework (JCF). With the JCF you can use classes such as `ArrayList` and `LinkedList` to create lists. Although these classes are provided for you, as a student of computer science it is important that you understand how list classes are implemented, and be able to write your own list classes.

#### **List Operations**

[Table 19-1](#dummy_split_026.html_filepos3062500) describes a set of common operations that most list classes can perform. These operations are for adding elements, getting elements, removing elements, and so forth. Note that the operations in [Table 19-1](#dummy_split_026.html_filepos3062500) are a subset of those specified by the `java.util.List` interface in the Java Collections Framework.

### **19.2 Creating an Array-Based List to Hold `String` Objects**

> **CONCEPT: An array-based list uses an internal array to hold list elements. An array-based list can be resizable, which means its internal array is automatically expanded when it is full and another element is added to the list**.

We will begin our study of lists by creating a list that can hold `String` objects. Our first step will be to design an interface that specifies all of the common list operations that are described in [Table 19-1](#dummy_split_026.html_filepos3062500). The interface, which is named `StringList`, is shown in the UML diagram in [Figure 19-1](#dummy_split_026.html_filepos3063803), and in [Code Listing 19-1](#dummy_split_026.html_filepos3064065).

**Figure 19-1** `StringList` interface

![Image](images/01407.jpg)

**Code Listing 19-1 `(StringList.java)`**

![Image](images/01408.jpg)

![Image](images/01409.jpg)

![Image](images/01410.jpg)

![Image](images/01411.jpg)

The `StringList` interface specifies the operations that we need to implement in our list of strings. It does not describe how those operations are carried out, however. Those details will be handled in a concrete class. When designing a concrete list class, we must decide how we will store the list elements in memory, and how we will carry out the list operations on those elements.

#### **Array-Based Lists and Resizable Lists**

There are various ways to store a list in memory. In this chapter, all of our concrete list classes will be array-based lists. An *array-based list* uses an internal array to store its list elements. Our concrete list classes will also be *resizable*, which means that their internal array is automatically expanded when it is full and another element is added to the list.

##### **Capacity**

A resizable array-based list has a capacity, which is different from its size. A list’s *capacity* is the number of elements it can store without having to be expanded. Its size, however, is the number of elements actually stored in the list. It is possible for a list’s internal array to be only partially filled, so a list’s size will always be less than or equal to its capacity. Its capacity will always be at least as big as its size.

The concrete list classes that we will create in this chapter will have a default initial capacity of 10 elements. This means that the list’s internal array will be initially created with a length of 10\. We will also provide constructors that allow you to specify other capacities. When a list’s internal array is full and another element is added to the list, the list class will automatically double the size of the array.

#### **A Concrete Class for Storing a List of Strings**

[Figure 19-2](#dummy_split_026.html_filepos3067370) shows a UML diagram for the `StringListType` class. This is a concrete class that implements the `StringList` interface. The design strategy of the class is to store the list in a resizable array.

**Figure 19-2** `StringListType` class

![Image](images/01412.jpg)

Because the `StringList` interface does not specify the details of how to implement a list, the class has a few additional methods. These are necessary to support a resizable array-based list. [Table 19-2](#dummy_split_026.html_filepos3068002) describes the additional methods.

##### **The Private Fields**

Looking at the UML diagram in [Figure 19-2](#dummy_split_026.html_filepos3067370), notice that the class has some private fields. Here are the declarations of these fields:

![Image](images/01414.jpg)

Lines 9 and 10 declare two `final int` variables. `DEFAULT_CAPACITY` is initialized with the value 10, which is the default capacity of the list. `RESIZE_FACTOR` is initialized with the value 2\. When the array is expanded, the new length of the array will be the current length multiplied by this value.

Line 13 declares `list`, which is a reference to a `String` array. The `list` field will reference the array that holds the list elements. Line 14 declares `elements`, an `int`. This field will hold the number of elements stored in the list.

##### **The Constructors**

The class provides two constructors. The first, shown here, is a no-arg constructor that creates an empty list with the default capacity:

![Image](images/01415.jpg)

Line 21 creates the list as an array of `String` references. The length of the array is the value stored in `DEFAULT_CAPACITY`, which is 10. Each element of the array has a `null` reference, so the list is empty. Line 22 initializes the `elements` field to 0\. This field will be updated each time an element is added to or removed from the list.

The second constructor, which accepts an `int` argument, is shown here:

![Image](images/01416.jpg)

The argument passed to the `capacity` parameter is used as the length of the array. Notice that this constructor throws an `IllegalArgumentException` if the argument is less than one.

##### **The `add` Methods**

The first `add` method accepts a `String` argument, and adds it to the end of the list as follows:

![Image](images/01417.jpg)

The `if` statement in line 46 determines whether the array is full. When it is, `elements` will be equal to the length of the list. If this is the case, the `resize` method is called to double the length of the array.

The second `add` method adds an element at a specific index. The value that is currently at that index, and all subsequent values, are shifted toward the end of the list as follows:

![Image](images/01418.jpg)

##### **The `clear` Method**

The `clear` method simply clears the list so it no longer contains any elements:

![Image](images/01419.jpg)

##### **The `contains` Method**

The `contains` method accepts a `String` argument and returns `true` if the argument is found in the list. If the argument is not in the list, the method returns `false`. Because the elements are not sorted, but stored in the order that they are added to the list, the method performs a sequential search as follows:

![Image](images/01420.jpg)

##### **The `get` Method**

The get method returns the string that is stored at a particular index. If an invalid index is specified, the method throws an IndexOutOfBoundsException as follows:

![Image](images/01421.jpg)

##### **The `indexOf` Method**

The `indexOf` method accepts a `String` argument. It searches the list for the `String`, and if it is found, its index is returned. If the `String` is not found in the list, the method returns −1\. As with the `contains` method, this method performs a sequential search because the list elements are not sorted in any particular order.

![Image](images/01422.jpg)

##### **The `isEmpty` Method**

The `isEmpty` method determines whether the list contains any elements. If the list is empty, it returns `true`. Otherwise, it returns `false`. The method works by returning the value of the expression `(elements == 0)` as follows:

![Image](images/01423.jpg)

##### **The `remove` Methods**

The class has two overloaded `remove` methods. The first `remove` method accepts a `String` argument. The loop in lines 174 through 182 searches the list for the `String`, and if it is found, it is removed from the list. When the element is removed, the loop in lines 188 through 192 shifts the subsequent elements one position toward the front of the list. If the `String` is found, and removed from the list, the method returns `true`. If the `String` is not found, the method returns `false`.

![Image](images/01424.jpg)

The second `remove` method removes an element at a specified index. Once the element is removed, the subsequent elements are shifted one position toward the front of the list. The method returns a reference to the element that was removed. If an invalid index is specified, the method throws an `IndexOutOfBoundsException` as follows:

![Image](images/01425.jpg)

##### **The `resize` Method**

The `resize` method is a private method that increases the length of the underlying array. The statement in line 238 calculates the new length of the array by multiplying its current length by `RESIZE_FACTOR`. Recall that `RESIZE_FACTOR` is 2, so the new length of the array will be twice its current length. Line 241 creates an array of the new length. The loop in lines 244 through 245 copies the current contents of the `list` array to the new array. Then, the statement in line 248 assigns the new array to the `list` variable as follows:

![Image](images/01426.jpg)

##### **The `set` Method**

The `set` method accepts an index and a `String` as arguments. It replaces the existing element at the specified index with the `String`. A reference to the `String` that was previously stored at the specified index is returned. If an invalid index is specified, the method throws an `IndexOutOfBoundsException` as follows:

![Image](images/01427.jpg)

##### **The `size` Method**

The `size` method returns the number of elements stored in the list as follows:

![Image](images/01428.jpg)

##### **The `toStringArray` Method**

The `toStringArray` method is a convenience method that returns a `String` array containing the elements of the list. We will use this method later in a GUI application to display the contents of the list in a `JList` component.

![Image](images/01429.jpg)

### **19.3 Creating a Generic Array-Based List**

> **CONCEPT: With generics we can create the interfaces and classes for a list that can hold objects of any type**.

In the previous sections we examined the `StringList` interface and the `StringListType` class. These are designed specifically for creating lists that store `String` objects. But what if we want to create lists to store other types of objects? One approach would be to create modified versions of the interface and class. A more practical approach, however, is to design our list using generics. If we use generics, our list does not have to be limited to a single type of object. In this section we will study a new interface and a new concrete class that use generics.

[Figure 19-6](#dummy_split_026.html_filepos3095192) and [Code Listing 19-4](#dummy_split_026.html_filepos3095455) show the `GeneralList` interface, which specifies the general operations of a list. (This file is stored in the source code folder *[Chapter 19](#dummy_split_026.html_filepos3058777)\Generic List Files.*) The `GeneralList` interface is a generic version of the `StringList` interface we saw in Section 19.1\. Notice that a generic type parameter, `E`, is specified in the `GeneralList` interface. Throughout the interface code we have used `E`, instead of `String`, as the element type.

![Image](images/00005.jpg)

* * *

**NOTE:** We are not required to use `E` as the name of our type parameter, but recall from [Chapter 17](#dummy_split_024.html_filepos2759847) that the name `E` is commonly used to represent the type of an element.

* * *

If you looked at the `ListType` class carefully, you probably noticed that we had to write some unusual code for instantiating the internal `list` array. Recall from [Chapter 17](#dummy_split_024.html_filepos2759847) that the Java compiler will not allow you to create an array of objects that are instances of a generic type. This is because arrays in Java carry internal information about the data type of their elements at runtime. Because of erasure, an array of generic class instances would not have the necessary runtime type information, so the compiler will not allow such arrays to be created. There is a workaround, however. Look at line 24 in the no-arg constructor:

![Image](images/01469.jpg)

The `list` field’s type is `E[]`. The statement in line 24 creates an array of `Object` references, and then casts it to `E[]` so it can be assigned to `list`. Although the statement works, it causes a compiler warning similar to the following to be displayed:

> `Note: ListType.java uses unchecked or unsafe operations.`
> `Note: Recompile with -Xlint:unchecked for details.`

Normally we should avoid compiler warnings whenever possible. In this case, however, the workaround is required, so we will consider the warning a necessary evil. We have to use this workaround also in lines 42 and 250.

The reason for using generics in the `ListType` class is so we can create lists of objects of any class. In order for objects to work correctly with all of the `ListType` methods, however, they must override the `equals` method and the `toString` method. For example, look at lines 112 and 113 in the `contains` method:

![Image](images/01470.jpg)

The `if` statement calls a list element’s `equals` method to determine whether it is equal to another object that was passed as an argument. This is also done in the `indexOf` method (line 149), and the `remove` method (line 182). The `toString` method should be overridden because the `toStringArray` method calls it for each element of the list (line 303).

### **19.4 Writing Iterator Classes and Iterable Lists**

> **CONCEPT: You can write your own `Iterator` classes that work with your list classes**.

An *iterator* is an object that can be used to retrieve the elements from a list, one after the other. You typically use an iterator in a loop. During each repetition of the loop, the iterator retrieves a different element from the list.

We first discussed iterators in [Chapter 18](#dummy_split_025.html_filepos2894334). Recall that the collection classes in the Java Collections Framework provide an `iterator` method that returns an `Iterator` object. The `Iterator` object that is returned from this method can be used to iterate over all the elements in a collection. You can also equip your own list class with an `iterator` method that returns an `Iterator` object. The `Iterator` object that is returned can be used to iterate over the elements in your list class.

In order to use `Iterator`s with your list class, you must do two things:

> • Write a class that can be used to instantiate the iterator. The class must implement the `Iterator` interface. `Iterator` is in the `java.util` package.

> • Make your list class implement the `Iterable` interface. `Iterable` is in the `java.lang` package.

Once you have correctly done both of these, you can get an `Iterator` object from your list class and use that object to traverse your list. Let’s take a closer look at each of these steps.

#### **Writing an `Iterator` Class**

An `Iterator` class is one that implements the `java.util.Iterator` interface. This interface specifies the basic operations that an iterator must perform. [Figure 19-10](#dummy_split_026.html_filepos3111605) shows a UML diagram for the `Iterator` interface, and [Table 19-3](#dummy_split_026.html_filepos3111888) describes the methods it specifies.

![Image](images/00009.jpg)

**Table 19-3** Methods specified by the `Iterator` interface

[Code Listing 19-8](#dummy_split_026.html_filepos3112584) shows an example of an `Iterator` class. This class can be used to create iterators for our `ListType` class. (This file is stored in the source code folder *[Chapter 19](#dummy_split_026.html_filepos3058777)\Iterable List Files.*)

**Code Listing 19-8 `(ListTypeIterator.java)`**

![Image](images/01481.jpg)

![Image](images/01482.jpg)

![Image](images/01483.jpg)

![Image](images/01484.jpg)

Three fields are defined in lines 8 through 10\. The `list` field, defined in line 8, holds a reference to the list that we are traversing. The previous field, defined in line 9, holds the index of the previous element that was returned from the iterator. The `canRemove` field, defined in line 10, is a `boolean` field that indicates whether a call to the `remove` method can be executed.

The constructor appears in lines 15 through 26\. It accepts as an argument a reference to the list we are iterating over. This reference is assigned to the `list` field in line 18\. In line 21 we initialize the `previous` field with −1\. Each time we call `next` to retrieve an element, the `previous` field will be incremented to give us the index of the element to return. By initializing `previous` with −1, we know that the first call to `next` will return element 0\. In line 25 we initialize the `canRemove` field with `false`. Because `next` has not yet been called, we cannot use the `remove` method to remove an element from the list.

The `hasNext` method appears in lines 32 through 42\. It returns `true` if there are more elements in the list. The expression `(previous + 1)` gives us the index of the element that will be returned when the `next` method is called. If this value is less than the size of the list, then there is at least one more element to be returned.

The `next` method appears in lines 47 through 63\. This method returns the next element in the list. First it checks to see if there are more elements to return (line 50). If not, it throws a `NoSuchElementException`. If there are more elements, `previous` is incremented in line 55\. This gives us the index of the next element in the list. Line 59 sets the `canRemove` field to `true`, which indicates that the `remove` method can be called. Then, line 62 returns the element.

The `remove` method appears in lines 68 through 83\. This method removes the element that was returned by the most recent call to the `next` method. This method can only be called after `next` has been called, and can only be called once per call to `next`. The `if` statement in line 71 determines whether the `canRemove` field is set to `false`. If it is, then the method cannot be legally called, so an `InvalidStateException` is thrown. Otherwise, the statement in line 75 removes the previously returned list element. The `previous` field is decremented in line 78, and the `canRemove` field is set to `false` in line 82\. Setting `canRemove` to `false` ensures that the `remove` method cannot be called again until the `next` method is called.

#### **In the Spotlight: Array-based Lists in Computer Systems Software** ![Image](images/00008.jpg)

A computer operating system needs to keep track of many different types of collections. For example, the system must maintain a list of user names and passwords, a list of currently logged-in users, a list of attached disks, lists of folders or directories on each disk, and lists of files or subfolders in a given folder. Some of these lists are array-based lists.

You can use the `java.io.File` class to access file and file system–related information on your computer. The `File` class, first introduced in [Chapter 13](#dummy_split_020.html_filepos2257796), is an abstract representation of a file or directory (a directory in considered to be a special type of file). Here are some of the methods provided by this class:

`    boolean isDirectory()`
`    String[] list()`
`    static File[] listRoots()`
`    String getName()`

The first of these is an instance method that checks whether the `File` object is a directory. The second, also an instance method, returns `null` if the `File` instance on which it is called is not a directory; otherwise it returns a listing of the `File` objects contained in the directory. The `listRoots` method returns an array of `File` objects corresponding to the root file systems. In Microsoft Windows, these are the root directories on the disks attached to the computer. The `getName` method returns the name of the file or directory.

[Code Listing 19-11](#dummy_split_026.html_filepos3126028) illustrates the use of these methods. The output shows the result of running the program on a Microsoft Windows computer with a floppy drive A:\, a hard disk C:\, and a DVD writer D:\.
